The Crowned cormorant (Microcarbo coronatus) is a medium-sized coastal seabird endemic to the cold, productive waters of the Benguela upwelling system off southwestern Africa. Detailed studies of its reproductive biology in the laboratory indicate that females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with a maximum of three nesting attempts per year [F_R_i = three nesting attempts per year], a strategy that reflects the relatively low annual reproductive output typical of the family Phalacrocoracidae. Egg development proceeds under tightly controlled thermal conditions; at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryo completes its development and the chick hatches after an average period of 22.4 days [ab = 22.4 days]. This incubation period is consistent with the altricial mode of development seen in related species, where hatchlings emerge with minimal down and are entirely dependent on parental provisioning. The resulting neonate, wet from the egg, registers a very modest body mass of 13.6 grams [Wwb = 13.6 grams] at the moment of hatching, a value that reflects the trade-off between producing a viable chick and the energetic constraints of the incubating adult.

Following hatching, the altricial nestling enters a rapid developmental phase that is metabolically supported by a consistently elevated core body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], which is typical of active, endothermic avian chicks. Under these thermal conditions, the fledgling stage is attained quite rapidly; the time since birth at fledging has been recorded at 35 days [tx = 35 days], marking the age at which the young bird achieves its initial flight feathers and begins short, clumsy flights away from the nest site. at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]This developmental tempo is relatively compressed compared to other seabirds of similar size, likely because of the strong selective pressure from terrestrial predators along the Namibian coast. After reaching fledgling independence, the immature bird enters a long juvenile phase during which it must refine its foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body reserves. The capacity for rapid skeletal and muscular growth during the nestling period is substantial; adult asymptotic body mass, or ultimate wet weight, in this species averages 790 grams [Wwi = 790 grams], though males are on average slightly smaller, weighing approximately 725 grams. This substantial increase from the 13.6 gram hatchling mass represents a more than fifty-fold gain, a growth trajectory that underscores the efficiency of parental provisioning on a diet of small fish and cephalopods.

Puberty, defined here as the onset of functional gonadal activity, is not reached until well after the fledgling has dispersed and assumed an independent existence. At the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the process of sexual maturation is completed and puberty is attained at 105 days since birth [tp = 105 days since birth]. This relatively late onset of reproductive capability, occurring many weeks post-fledging, likely reflects the need for the juvenile to acquire the advanced foraging proficiency and social status required to secure a breeding territory and a mate. The discrepancy between the early fledging age and the delayed pubertal stage is a common life-history pattern among long-lived seabirds, which prioritize somatic development and skill acquisition over precocious reproduction. Even after reaching puberty, first-time breeders typically defer their initial reproductive attempt until the following breeding season, as the physiological and behavioral demands of successful nesting are considerable. The species thus exhibits a classic "slow" life history, characterized by a delayed return on reproductive investment and a prolonged pre-reproductive phase.

The initiation of the very first breeding event, representing the age at which a female successfully produces her first brood, occurs considerably later than the attainment of simple gonadal maturity. Field observations and recapture data from marked colonies indicate that, at the species' typical core temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the time since birth at the first brood is 730 days [tR = 730 days]. This two-year delay between hatching and first successful reproduction is a well-documented pattern in Microcarbo coronatus and other related cormorants, and it is thought to be driven by the time required to establish a stable position within a dense breeding colony and to refine the complex social and foraging behaviors needed for chick rearing. The reproductive career of an individual is therefore shaped by a long period of somatic and behavioral preparation. The consequence of this delayed breeding schedule, combined with the limited annual output of one egg per clutch and a maximum of three clutches per year, is a relatively low maximum lifetime reproductive rate.

Longevity records for this species, extrapolated from data on closely related congeners in the genus Phalacrocorax available through the AnAge database, suggest a considerable maximum lifespan. At the species' typical active body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the maximum documented lifespan is approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years], a value that positions the Crowned cormorant among the longer-lived members of the cormorant family. This extended longevity, coupled with the low annual reproductive output and delayed first breeding, reinforces the interpretation of Microcarbo coronatus as a classic K-selected species adapted to a stable but resource-limited marine environment. The slow life history is further reflected in the modest asymptotic body mass: as noted earlier, adult individuals typically approach an ultimate wet weight of 790 grams [Wwi = 790 grams], and the slight sexual dimorphism seen in males, which average around 725 grams, is consistent with a system where both sexes share parental duties equally. The interplay of a 35-day fledging period, a 105-day maturation to puberty, a 730-day delay to first reproduction, and a 25-year lifespan creates a demographic profile that is exceptionally sensitive to adult mortality, a factor that must be carefully considered in conservation planning for this range-restricted Benguela endemic.
